name: Kalabari-Ijo
catalog_citation: Harry, Otelemate G. 2003. Kalabari-Ijo (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 33(1): 113-120. doi:10.1017/S002510030300121X (Cambridge Core open PDF).
catalog_quote: Kalab.ari. is a tone language with two tone levels, high, / !/ and low, / Ÿ/. In addition, a phonemic downstep, [Õ !], occurs, which can give rise to a three-way contrast in morphemes, for example, /ı́kú/ 'lice' /ı́Õkú/ 'heavy' /ı́kù/ 'cocoyam' Further, downdrift occurs in Kalab.ari., whereby in an utterance any successive high tone is on a pitch lower than a preceding high due to an assimilatory effect of a surface intervening low tone (Jenewari 1977, Harry 1998). Similarly, downstep is underlyingly a high tone lowered by a preceding unassociated low tone in Kalab.ari.. All tones will be marked in broad and narrow transcriptions of the illustrative passage. In the orthographic rendition of the passage, high tone will be marked with the acute accent, downstep with a macron and low tone left unmarked, following the present orthographic conventions for Kalab.ari. (Jenewari 1978).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held Cambridge Core text layer of Harry 2003 at pp.118-119 'Tone system'; the article never uses the word 'stress'. (2) Deciding source is a 2003 JIPA Illustration by the language's principal phonologist; held corroboration from Harry & Hyman 2014 (H vs L lexical tones + downstep, construction-assigned phrasal melodies; 'stress' only in typological contrasts) and newly fetched sources Rolle & Harry 2025 PDA (p.4: basic L/H contrast + downstepped H, all morphemes fully specified for tone; no Kalabari stress rule). (3) The one materially fuller source, Harry 2004 CSLI tone monograph, is not open (publisher page checked; e-book ISBN only) and by all citing summaries describes the same H/L+downstep system; Jenewari 1977/1980 are print-only and older.

sources.citation: Rolle, Nicholas & Otelemate G. Harry. 2025. Why spread? Kalabari clitics spread their tone due to word-minimality, prosodic constituency, and *LHH tonotactics. Phonological Data and Analysis 7(2): 1-35. doi:10.3765/pda.v7art2.82 (CC BY 3.0, Cambridge Core OA PDF).
sources.quote: "Kalabari has a basic contrast between low (L) and high (H) tone. Downstepped high tones (i.e. ꜜH) also occur in some underlying and derived contexts, discussed separately in §2.4. All lexical morphemes and most functional morphemes are fully specified for tone on all tone-bearing units." No word-stress or accent rule for Kalabari anywhere in the 35 pp.; the words 'stress' occur only in cross-linguistic remarks on tone-prominence affinity (Köhnlein 2013, de Lacy 2002).
sources.locator: p.4, section 2.2 'Tone system' (txt lines 310-333); 'stress' only in typological asides pp.17-18 and reference titles
